module_doc:
# Checking a Boolean circuit certificate

The CLRS4 section 34.3 verifier (printed pages 1067-1068) checks every gate
against a supplied input-and-gate valuation and checks the designated output.
The counted events are the length check, each argument visit, each gate equality
check and the final output check; allocation and bit-machine costs are separate.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.Circuit.Verification

module_doc:
# Adjacency matrices

An `AdjacencyMatrix n` is a finite directed graph on vertices `Fin n`,
represented by a Boolean edge predicate `adj : Fin n → Fin n → Bool` behind a
structure wrapper. The operations are the empty graph, edge insertion and
deletion at a single ordered pair, an edge query `hasEdge`, and the
out-neighborhood `neighbors m i` as a list of vertices in increasing order.

The main statements are the pointwise characterizations of insertion and
deletion (`hasEdge_addEdge`, `hasEdge_eraseEdge`, and their off-pair variants)
and the agreement of the neighbor list with the edge query
(`mem_neighbors`). No complexity bounds are proved.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.AdjacencyMatrix

module_doc:
# AVL trees

This module develops height-balanced binary search trees with a cached height at
each node. The smart constructor `mkNode` recomputes the cache from the cached
heights of the children in constant time. Insertion repairs the balance invariant
with single and double rotations, all performed by the local rebalancing function
`balance`. Insertion ignores an already-present key.

Membership, `All`, ordering, and inorder traversal are not redeveloped here: they
are inherited from `BinarySearchTree` through the cache-erasing projection
`toBinaryTree`, as in `OrderStatisticTree`. Only the height caches, the balance
invariant, rotations, and the rebalancing insertion are AVL-specific; their
specifications are the erasure equations `inorder_balance`, `mem_balance`, and
`ordered_balance` together with the height bounds for `balance`.

Deletion is out of scope for this module.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.AvlTree

module_doc:
# AVL tree deletion

Deletion for the height-balanced binary search trees of
`CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.AvlTree`. Deletion follows the search
path exactly as in an ordinary binary search tree and rebuilds every node on
that path with the rebalancing function `balance` from the parent module. A
deleted node with at most one child is replaced by that child. A deleted node
with two children is replaced by the minimum key of its right subtree, with
that minimum removed by `eraseMin`. Deletion can shrink the height of the
affected subtree by at most one, so at each rebuilt node the two children
differ in height by at most two, which is exactly the precondition of
`balanced_balance`.

module_doc:
# B-trees

This module develops B-trees as in CLRS Chapter 18, with set semantics: a tree stores a
finite set of keys, and insertion of an already-present key leaves the tree unchanged.

A raw tree is either a leaf holding a list of keys or an internal node holding a list of
separator keys and a list of children. For minimum degree `t`, the invariant `Valid t mink h`
states that `h` is the height (leaves have height `0` and every leaf occurs at depth `h`, so
the tree is perfectly balanced), every node has at most `2 * t - 1` keys, every non-root node
has at least `t - 1` keys (the root instead satisfies the bound `mink`), and every internal
node with `k` keys has exactly `k + 1` children. The ordering invariant `Ordered` states
that the inorder flattening is strictly increasing; `Ordered.node_keys_pairwise` and
`Ordered.separator_bounds` extract from it the usual facts that the keys at each node are
sorted and that every key in a subtree lies strictly between the separators adjacent to it.

Insertion is a bottom-up, split-returning (overflow-returning) variant: the internal
function `ins` first inserts into a leaf or child, allowing a node to reach `2 * t` keys, and
splits such an overflowing node while returning, yielding either a single tree of the same
height or a pair of trees of the same height together with the median key promoted between
them; `insert` grows a new root exactly when the old root splits. This is not the insertion
algorithm of CLRS (Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, and Stein, *Introduction to Algorithms*, 3rd
edition, §18.2), which is top-down: it splits every full `2 * t - 1`-key node before
descending into it, so no overflow ever arises. The deviation affects tree shape: for
`t = 2`, inserting `0` into the leaf `[1, 2, 3]` promotes `1` here (the median of the
overflow `[0, 1, 2, 3]`), where CLRS first promotes `2` (splitting `[1, 2, 3]` before
descending). The B-tree invariants and set semantics agree with CLRS Chapter 18; only the
insertion strategy (and hence the resulting shape) differs.
The main lemmas are that `flatten (insert t x tr) = orderedInsert x (flatten tr)` for a valid
ordered tree, that insertion preserves validity and orderedness, and that the search
procedure `contains` agrees with membership.

Deletion is out of scope for this module.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BTree

module_doc:
# B-tree deletion by rebuilding

Rebuild-based deletion for the B-trees of
`CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BTree`, with the same set
semantics as insertion there: deleting an absent key leaves the stored
set unchanged. The primary deletion operation is `delete` in the sibling
module `CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BTree.DeleteBalanced`
(the top-down CLRS 18.3 descent); `deleteRebuild` here is retained as a
reference implementation whose specification is immediate from the
builder.

## What is implemented, and what is not

`deleteRebuild t x tree` is defined by erasing `x` from the inorder
flattening and rebuilding a tree from the remaining keys with `fromList`,
the genuine B-tree builder of the parent module (a fold of the parent
module's bottom-up split-returning insertion, whose invariant is
`IsBTree.fromList`; that insertion is an overflow-returning variant, not
the top-down insertion of CLRS §18.2, 3rd edition, see the parent
module's documentation). The results below are therefore exact at the
level of the parent module's specification:

* `flatten_deleteRebuild`: the flattening of the result is exactly
  `(flatten tree).erase x`, for an ordered tree with `2 ≤ t`;
* `IsBTree.deleteRebuild`: the result is again a B-tree, that is, it is ordered and
  root-valid at some height, so the occupancy bounds (at most `2 * t - 1`
  keys at every node, at least `t - 1` at every non-root node) and the
  uniform-height condition of `Valid`/`ValidRoot` hold for the result by
  construction;
* `mem_deleteRebuild` and `contains_deleteRebuild_iff`: membership and search agree with
  deletion from the stored set.

This is not the single-pass CLRS 18.3 deletion. There is no descent that
borrows a key from a sibling or merges a child with a separator before
recursing, and no claim is made here that the height of the result differs
from the height of the input only by a root merge: the height is whatever
height the rebuilt tree of the remaining keys has, subject only to
`ValidRoot`. The cost is correspondingly the rebuild cost. Evaluating
`flatten tree` is linear in the number of stored keys (`flattenAux`
prepends each key once), erasing from the materialized flattening is
linear, and rebuilding inserts every remaining key; each insertion
performs `O(t)` list work at each of `O(log_t n)` levels, so the rebuild
is `O(n · t · log_t n)` when `t` is counted as a parameter
(`Θ(n log_t n)` insertions only at fixed `t`), not the `O(t log_t n)` of
the CLRS descent. The single-pass borrow/merge algorithm, with its height
statement (the height decreases only when the root's two children merge),
is `delete` in
`CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BTree.DeleteBalanced`; this
module supplies the rebuild reference and its invariant on top of the
proved builder.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BTree.Delete

module_doc:
# B-tree deletion by a top-down pass

Top-down deletion for the B-trees of
`CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BTree`, following CLRS
Section 18.3. Unlike `deleteRebuild` in the sibling module
`CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BTree.Delete` (the declaration
`Cslib.Algorithms.Lean.BTree.deleteRebuild`), which erases the key from
the flattening and rebuilds the tree by insertion, `delete` here descends
from the root to a leaf, repairing occupancy along the way. This `delete`
is the primary deletion operation for B-trees; `deleteRebuild` is retained
as a reference implementation with the same set semantics.
Predecessor and successor keys are found by descending a single spine
(`maxKey`/`minKey`), never by flattening a subtree. Deleting a separator
key therefore traverses that spine twice: `maxKey` (dually `minKey`)
first descends the rightmost (leftmost) spine of the child to read the
predecessor (successor), and the recursive deletion then descends the
same spine again to remove it. The total is still `O(t * height)` list
cells, matching the CLRS bound up to the list representation of nodes,
but the separator case is not literally a single root-to-leaf pass.

The descent maintains the CLRS precondition that every node entered (other
than the root) holds at least `t` keys: before descending into a child with
only `t - 1` keys, `delList` either borrows a key for it from an adjacent
sibling with at least `t` keys (`borrowRight`/`borrowLeft`: the separator
moves down into the child and the sibling's nearest key moves up), or merges
the child with the separator and the sibling into one node with `2 * t - 1`
keys (`merge`). A separator key itself is deleted by promoting its
predecessor or successor when the corresponding child has at least `t`
keys, and by merging its two children otherwise. The recursion is indexed
by height (`delH`), so a merged node is deleted from at the children's
height. The public `delete` collapses the root when a root merge leaves
it with no keys and a single child, the only way the height decreases
(`delete_validRoot`).

The specifications are `flatten_delete` (the flattening of the result is
`(flatten tree).erase x`), `IsBTree.delete` (the result is ordered and
root-valid), and the height statement `delete_validRoot` (the result is
root-valid at the height of the input or one less).
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BTree.DeleteBalanced

module_doc:
# Ball trees

This file defines a simplified verified bounding-sphere (ball) tree for
similarity search. Points are functions `Fin d → Int`, and similarity
is measured by the squared Euclidean distance `distSq`, a natural number,
so neither real numbers nor square roots occur. Each internal node stores
a bounding sphere: a center point and a squared-radius bound covering
every point in the subtree, which is the invariant `Valid`. Leaves hold a
single point. Building splits the point list in half recursively, taking
the first point as the sphere center and the largest squared distance
from it as the bound. The similarity (range) search for a query point and
a squared radius prunes a subtree whose bounding sphere is provably
disjoint from the query ball, via the squared-distance estimate
`distSq a c ≤ 2 * (distSq a b + distSq b c)` in `distSq_le_two_mul`, and
the main theorem states that the search of a valid tree is exactly its
point list filtered by the distance predicate.

## Main definitions

* `BallTree.distSq` is squared Euclidean distance over `Fin d → Int`.
* `BallTree.build` builds a tree by recursive halving.
* `BallTree.search` lists the points of the tree within a squared radius of
  a query point.

## Deferred

Bounded fanout and multi-point leaves, centroid- or variance-based split
heuristics, dynamic insertion with node splitting, nearest-neighbor
search, and all complexity bounds are not proved here; no cost model is
carried.

This is a binary ball tree only. It is not an SS-tree: the bounded-fanout
multiway nodes, centroid-and-radius directory entries, occupancy bounds,
and variance-based node splitting that define SS-trees are all deferred
above, and SS-trees remain a separate coverage gap.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BallTree

module_doc:
# Fixed-width binary counter

Increment and run formalize the CLRS binary counter, fourth edition, Section 16.1, pages 451-453.
Supplemental reset uses the same representation and charges true-to-false bit changes.

## Main statements

Increment has unsigned modular value and exact initial-one-prefix cost. Successive
increments have modular value, exact per-position flip counts from zero, and actual
total cost equal to the sum of those counts. A positive-length zero-start run costs
strictly less than twice its length, and a positive-width run costs at least its length.

## Implementation notes

Each cleared or set existing bit costs one tick. Testing, traversal, conversions,
persistent copying, allocation, machine/word/bit complexity and space are excluded.
Width zero is legal and has zero cost. All-one input wraps without a new high bit.
Proof-only observers and carry machinery remain private.
Authored by Codex at Adam Kiezun's explicit selection.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BinaryCounter

module_doc:
# Binary min-heaps

This file defines a binary min-heap backed by a level-order array. Sifting swaps entries only
along one ancestor or descendant path. The public theorems prove local heap order, global root
minimality, permutation laws, and exact multiplicity behavior for insertion and extraction.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BinaryHeap

module_doc:
# Binary-heap sift-up event bounds

The cost coordinates count value comparisons and actual swaps, respectively.
Bounds checks, reads, copying, allocation, calls, and comparator implementation costs are free
in this model. These are execution-linked event bounds, not physical running-time bounds.
The canonical heap representation and operations are unchanged.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BinaryHeap.Cost

module_doc:
# Decrease-key for binary min-heaps

This file decreases one indexed key and repairs the affected ancestor path.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BinaryHeap.DecreaseKey

module_doc:
# One-pass sift-down event costs

The counters record value comparisons and actual array swaps, not elapsed time.
Erasing counters gives canonical sift-down without a heap-order precondition.
Bounds use the remaining depth `Nat.log2 a.size - Nat.log2 (i + 1)`.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BinaryHeap.SiftDownCost

module_doc:
# Binary search trees

This module develops pure, unbalanced binary search trees directly over Mathlib's
`BinaryTree`. Insertion ignores an already-present key. `rank` and `select` are
traversal specifications and do not claim cached order-statistic navigation.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BinarySearchTree

module_doc:
# Binary search tree deletion

Deletion for the pure, unbalanced binary search trees of
`CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BinarySearchTree`. When the deleted
key sits at a node, its two subtrees are spliced together with `join`, so a
leaf or one-child node is replaced by its remaining subtree and a two-child
node by the concatenation of both. Membership of every other key is preserved
for arbitrary trees; that the deleted key itself disappears, that `Ordered`
is preserved, and the traversal specification `inorder_delete` assume the
strict invariant `Ordered`, matching `contains_eq_true_iff` in the parent
module.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BinarySearchTree.Delete

module_doc:
# Binomial min-heaps

This module implements persistent binomial trees and forests. A valid tree of rank `r` has
children of ranks `r - 1, ..., 0`, contains exactly `2 ^ r` elements, and has a root no greater
than any represented element. A valid heap is a forest whose tree ranks are strictly increasing.

`BinomialTree.link` retains its left argument as parent when the roots compare equal. The same
left-biased policy is used when selecting the minimum tree.

The machine-checked results establish the rank, size, order, forest, and multiset invariants.
There is no formal cost model here. Under constant-time comparison and constructor assumptions,
`link` takes constant time; insertion and minimum inspection visit at most the number of roots
`k`; and the implementation gives conservative worst-case bounds `O((k₁ + k₂) ^ 2)` for
meld and `O(k + r + (k + r) ^ 2)` for deleting a tree of rank `r`. The proved powers-of-two tree
sizes and unique ranks give machine-checked binary-logarithm bounds on `k` and `r`.
These structural bounds are not theorems about running time in this module.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BinomialHeap

module_doc:
# Bloom filters

A Bloom filter over `α` is a bit vector of length `m` together with a list of hash functions
`α → Fin m`, following the presentation in La Rocca, *Advanced Algorithms and Data Structures*,
Chapter 4. Inserting an element sets the bit selected by every hash function, and `mayContain`
reports whether all of those bits are set.

## Main definitions

* `BloomFilter` packages the hash functions with the bit vector.
* `BloomFilter.empty`, `BloomFilter.insert`, and `BloomFilter.mayContain` are the operations.

## Main statements

Bits are only ever set, never cleared, so membership answers have no false negatives:
`mayContain_insert_self` and the monotonicity statement `mayContain_insert_mono`. The exact set
of bits set after an insertion is `bit_insert_iff`. No false-positive probability is claimed:
the model supplies no distribution on elements or hashes.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.BloomFilter

module_doc:
# Cartesian trees

The Cartesian tree of a list is the binary tree whose inorder traversal is the
list itself and which is heap-ordered by value: the root is the minimum element,
the left subtree is built from the elements before that minimum, and the right
subtree from the elements after it. This is the treap view of an array: with
priorities in place of values it is the structure behind randomized search trees
and range-minimum queries (La Rocca, *Advanced Algorithms and Data Structures*,
ch. 3; Demaine, MIT 6.851, Lecture 15).

`build` recursively splits its input at the (first) minimum. Recursion is on an
explicit fuel initialized to the input length; each split produces strictly
shorter lists, so the fuel bound `xs.length ≤ n` maintained in the correctness
proofs is exactly termination by list length. When the minimum occurs several
times, splitting at its first occurrence still yields a heap-ordered tree with
the correct inorder traversal.

The machine-checked results are `inorder_build` (the inorder traversal of
`build xs` is `xs`), `heapOrdered_build` (the result satisfies the recursive
`HeapOrdered` predicate), `root_build_min` (the root is a minimum of the input),
and `perm_build` (the elements are a permutation of the input). The split
helper is specified by `splitAtFirst_spec` (reconstruction from the two
parts) together with `splitAtFirst_not_mem_fst` (the split value does not
occur in the left part, i.e. the split is at its first occurrence). No cost model is
formalized; this splitting construction takes quadratic time in the worst case,
while the classic stack-based construction is linear.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.CartesianTree

module_doc:
# Cuckoo hashing

A cuckoo hash table (Demaine, MIT 6.851 *Advanced Data Structures*, Lecture 10) keeps two
tables of `m` slots each and two hash functions `h1 h2 : K → Fin m`. A key `k` may only ever
sit in `table1[h1 k]` or in `table2[h2 k]`, so `lookup` checks exactly those two slots.
Insertion first overwrites an existing binding for the key in place; otherwise it runs the
eviction loop: write the new pair into `table1[h1 k]`, move the evicted occupant to its
other slot, and so on, alternating tables. The loop is bounded by an explicit fuel and
returns `none` on exhaustion, which models the trigger for a rehash; rehashing itself is
not modeled.

## Main definitions

* `CuckooHashing` stores the two slot vectors.
* `CuckooHashing.empty`, `CuckooHashing.lookup`, and `CuckooHashing.insert` are the
  operations; `insert` takes a fuel bound and returns an `Option` table.
* `CuckooHashing.Valid` is the placement invariant: every stored entry sits at `h1` of its
  key in the first table or at `h2` of its key in the second.
* `CuckooHashing.Stored` says a binding occurs in some slot of either table, and
  `CuckooHashing.KeyDet` says each key is stored with at most one value.

## Main statements

A successful insertion preserves `Valid` and `KeyDet` (`valid_insert`, `keyDet_insert`) and
stores the inserted binding. Lookup is sound
unconditionally (a found value is stored) and complete under `Valid`: a stored key is
found, and under the additional `KeyDet` it is found with its stored value. Under `Valid`
and `KeyDet`, looking up a successfully inserted key returns the inserted value. No
expected constant-time bound is claimed: the model supplies no probability distribution or
independence assumption on `h1` and `h2`, and insert failure is possible for any fuel.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.CuckooHashing

module_doc:
# Configurable-arity min-heaps

This file defines a min-heap backed by a contiguous level-order array. A requested arity below
two is normalized to two. For arity `d`, the parent of nonroot index `i` is `(i - 1) / d`, and
the child with zero-based offset `k` is `d * i + k + 1`.

Insertion appends once and sifts along the genuine `d`-ary ancestor path. Extraction moves the
last entry to the root and sifts it down along a single `d`-ary child path, choosing the smallest
valid child at each step. The representation stores exactly one array entry per multiset
occurrence, plus one natural-number arity field and proofs erased by Lean's compiler.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.DaryHeap

module_doc:
# Double-ended queues

A `Deque` is represented by two lists. The `front` list stores the front part of the sequence
in order, so its head is the frontmost element. The `back` list stores the back part of the
sequence in reverse order, so its head is the backmost element. The represented sequence is
therefore `front ++ back.reverse`.

Pushing at either end conses onto the corresponding list. Popping at an end whose list is
empty reverses the other list, following Lean's two-list `Std.Queue`; peeking at such an end
only traverses the other list with `getLast?` and allocates nothing. This file proves
that every operation agrees with the represented sequence; it makes no complexity claims.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.Deque

module_doc:
# Doubly-linked list prepend with pointer-event costs

`Node` has an identity-independent payload and optional next/previous pointers.
`Represents` relates a finite allocated node pool and header to an ordered list
of distinct node identities. `listPrepend` implements CLRS fourth edition,
section 10.2, printed page 260, LIST-PREPEND, including its update order.

The caller supplies an allocated node, not an allocator. Execution requires
only access to that node and any old head. Freshness is a representation-proof
premise, not an execution premise. The nonempty branch reads the carried store
after both writes at the supplied node, even when that node is the old head.

The same computation counts one event per pointer assignment and per old-head
NIL test: four events for an empty header, five otherwise. Array indexing,
record reads, erased proofs and return are free in this model. These are not
claims about native constant time, physical allocation, space or full RAM cost.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.DoublyLinkedList.Basic

module_doc:
# Doubly linked list deletion

CLRS fourth edition, section 10.2, printed page 261, `LIST-DELETE`.
The supplied node remains allocated; only its predecessor, successor and header
are spliced. Costs count NIL tests and executed pointer assignments, not physical
RAM accesses, persistent-store copies or native execution time.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.DoublyLinkedList.Delete

module_doc:
# Doubly-linked list insertion with pointer-event costs

CLRS fourth edition, section 10.2, printed page 261, LIST-INSERT.
An already allocated node is inserted after an allocated node in the source's
five-line order. Each update reads the carried store, including aliased targets.
Freshness is a representation-proof premise, not an execution guard.

The same computation counts executed pointer assignments and the successor NIL
test: four events at the tail, five otherwise. Indexing, record reads, erased
proofs and return are free. This is not physical RAM, persistent-copy, word/bit,
allocation, native execution-time or space complexity.

The return and pointwise equations preserve access-valid aliases. Canonical
`Represents` insertion uses `List.insertIdx`; another disjoint represented
list is preserved by the same store's frame theorem.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.DoublyLinkedList.Insert

module_doc:
# Circular doubly-linked lists with an allocated sentinel

CLRS fourth edition, section 10.2, printed pages 261–262. The sentinel replaces
NIL and links the first and last data nodes, or links to itself for an empty list.
The same canonical node pool supports several disjoint represented circles.
Payloads are unrestricted; the sentinel is an allocated node, not another carrier.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.DoublyLinkedList.Sentinel.Basic

module_doc:
# Deletion from a circular doubly-linked list with a sentinel

CLRS fourth edition, section 10.2, printed page 262, LIST-DELETE-prime.
The actual computation performs both pointer assignments in source order and
rereads the successor from the carried store. The selected record stays allocated.
Allocation access is the execution domain; sentinel exclusion and list membership
are representation-proof premises, not new runtime guards.

The same canonical TimeM computation counts exactly two pointer assignments, even
for access-valid aliases. This metric excludes physical RAM accesses, persistent
store copying, allocation, bit cost, space and native execution time.

Private proof support relates the exact circular predicate to List.IsChain and
reuses canonical listDelete field laws through an exact return bridge. The actual
executor does not call listDelete. Generic erasure is ids.erase x and disjointness
includes both sentinels in their corresponding address lists.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.DoublyLinkedList.Sentinel.Delete

module_doc:
# Sentinel insertion, CLRS4 section10.2 printed263

Exactly four carried-store assignments, one tick per actual write.
Access-valid aliases are allowed; freshness is a correctness premise only.
Private carried-store proof facts are adapted from landed U056 Insert.lean.
Its existing public field theorems will be reused only after actual-return equality.
No NIL test, allocation, head update, RAM/bit/space or native-time claim.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.DoublyLinkedList.Sentinel.Insert

module_doc:
# Sentinel linked-list search

CLRS fourth edition, section 10.2, printed page 263. The query is stored in the
allocated sentinel key before following actual next pointers until a key matches.
The final identity test distinguishes a data match from the sentinel failure stop.
Canonical circular representation and CSLib TimeM are reused directly.

The selected-event model charges write1, initialization1, comparison1 per visit,
advance1 per mismatch and final identity1. Reads, proof terms and result construction
are free. Physical RAM, persistent storage copying and word/bit costs are not claimed.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.DoublyLinkedList.Sentinel.Search

module_doc:
# Dynamic-table insertion

CLRS, fourth edition, Section 16.4.1, printed pages 461–464. Count one event
for each copied old item and for the new item write, not allocation or full RAM cost.
Retained Lean is authored by Codex at Adam Kiezun's explicit selection.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.DynamicTable.Basic

module_doc:
# Dynamic-table deletion and lookup

Deletion follows CLRS, fourth edition, Section 16.4.2: removing the last item
contracts the table to half capacity when the load factor drops below `1/4`.

Design choice: `tableDelete` is a pure `Table α → Table α`, not a `TimeM`
executor like `tableInsert` in `Basic`, because the timed copying routine
`copyItems` is private to `Basic`; a copy-cost account of deletion is deferred.
Contraction is implemented by rebuilding the slot array as the occupied prefix
followed by empty slots; without contraction the last slot is cleared in
place. Deleting the sole item of a one-slot table contracts to capacity zero,
matching the initially unallocated `empty` table of `Basic`.

`Basic` has no lookup operation, so this module also adds `get?`, indexed by
logical position.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.DynamicTable.Delete

module_doc:
# Euler tours of rooted trees

This file defines rooted ordered trees and their Euler tours. The `tour` of a tree
is the vertex sequence of a depth-first walk that returns to the parent after each
child subtree, so every tree edge is traversed twice, once in each direction. The
`arcTour` is the sequence of consecutively traversed arcs; a tree with `n` vertices
has tour length `2 * n - 1` and exactly `2 * (n - 1)` arcs.

Vertices need not be distinct in a raw `Tree`; the dynamic-forest reading
(placing vertices of one tree in another) requires the `Tree.Valid`
invariant (`vertices` duplicate-free) plus disjoint vertex sets for `link`,
recorded in `Tree.valid_link`. Without those hypotheses `link`/`tour` are
still total list operations on labelled trees, but they do not describe a
forest link.

Link and cut are recorded at the level of tours. `link t₁ t₂` attaches `t₂` as the
last child of the root of `t₁`, and its tour is the list splice
`tour t₁ ++ tour t₂ ++ [t₁.root]`: the tour of `t₁` is a prefix and the tour of `t₂`
occurs as a contiguous block. `cutLast` removes the last child subtree of the root
and inverts `link`. These are the sequence operations underlying Euler-tour trees
for dynamic forests.

Out of scope: balance and complexity (tours are plain lists here, so splicing is
linear in this representation, not the logarithmic bound of a balanced sequence),
subtree aggregate queries over tours, and the link-cut tree proper. The splay-based
link-cut tree is deferred until a splay tree module is present in this library; this
file provides the Euler-tour representation and its splice specification only.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.EulerTourTree

module_doc:
# Fenwick trees (binary indexed trees)

A Fenwick tree over an additive commutative monoid represents a zero-indexed
array by a one-indexed stored `Array` `bit` whose entry at `j ≥ 1` is the sum of
the `lowbit j` underlying entries ending at position `j - 1`. Only `bit` is
stored at runtime; the underlying array appears solely in the specification
relation `FenwickTree.Valid`. Prefix sums walk `k, k - lowbit k, …` down to `0`
reading stored entries in constant time, with query indices past the end clamped
like `List.take`. A point update walks `i + 1, j + lowbit j, …` and adds its
delta to exactly the stored entries on that walk. Each such write is
constant-time only when the stored array is uniquely referenced; if the
original tree is retained, Lean's persistent `Array.set` may first copy the
array in linear time, so a persistent update can cost `O(n + log n)`.

## Main definitions

* `FenwickTree.lowbit` is the largest power of two dividing its input.
* `FenwickTree.build` constructs the stored interval sums from an array.
* `FenwickTree.add`, `FenwickTree.prefixSum`, and `FenwickTree.rangeSum` are the operations.
* `FenwickTree.Valid t arr` says `t` represents `arr`: every stored entry
  equals its interval sum.

## Main statements

For a tree representing `arr`, `prefixSum` at every index (including past the
end) agrees with the sum of the corresponding `List.take` of `arr`, `rangeSum`
(the one operation needing additive inverses) agrees with the sum over the
corresponding interval, and `add` moves the representation to the point-updated
array and changes prefix sums exactly past the updated position. No logarithmic
cost bound is claimed: the model carries no cost instrumentation, although the
operations follow the usual logarithmic walks over an `Array`.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.FenwickTree

module_doc:
# Fibonacci min-heaps

This module implements persistent Fibonacci heaps following CLRS Chapter 19, in the
correctness-only style of `BinomialHeap.lean`. A heap is a list of heap-ordered trees together
with a cached minimum root value. Insertion and meld are lazy: they only add trees to the root
list and update the cached minimum. Deleting the minimum promotes the children of the minimum
tree and then consolidates the root list by repeatedly linking trees of equal degree, so the
resulting roots have strictly increasing degrees.

The core representation here omits marked nodes and cascading cuts; tree nodes store
only a degree, a root value, and children. A simplified `decreaseKey` operation that
does not perform cascading cuts lives in `FibonacciHeap.DecreaseKey`. The classical Fibonacci size bound
(count at least the `(degree + 2)`-nd Fibonacci number) is also deferred: it depends on
controlling the degrees of children through the mark/cut invariant of CLRS, while `Valid`
here records only heap order and `degree = children.length`. The size facts proved instead
are positivity of tree counts, `degree < count` for every valid tree, and the bound
`roots ≤ count` for consolidated forests.

There is no formal cost model here. The machine-checked results establish the heap-order,
cached-minimum, consolidation, and multiset invariants.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.FibonacciHeap

module_doc:
# Decrease-key for Fibonacci heaps: cut without marks

CLRS `FIB-HEAP-DECREASE-KEY` (Chapter 19) lowers the key of a node `x`, cuts `x` from
its parent if heap order is violated, and then performs cascading cuts: a parent that
has already lost one child since it was linked (it is marked) is itself cut, and so on
up the tree. The parent module `FibonacciHeap.lean` represents trees as persistent rose
trees storing only a degree, a root value, and children: there are no parent pointers
and no mark field, so the CLRS procedure cannot be implemented literally here. This
file implements the honest functional analogue and states plainly where it deviates.

The node to decrease is addressed by a path: a list of child indices from a root of the
forest (`FibonacciTree.subtreeAt`). A path is the persistent substitute for the node
handle that an imperative implementation passes to decrease-key; no parent pointers are
simulated. `FibonacciTree.cutAt` extracts the subtree at a path and rebuilds its
ancestors with corrected degrees, `FibonacciTree.decreaseRoot` lowers the extracted
root, and `FibonacciHeap.decreaseKey` puts the decreased subtree back as a new tree in
the root list. The cut is unconditional: the subtree moves to the root list even when
the decreased key would still respect heap order under its old parent. That is a
simplification, not a correctness issue.

What is missing, plainly: cascading cuts. Without a mark field there is no record of
how many children a node has lost since it was linked, so ancestors of a cut node are
never themselves cut, and a node can lose arbitrarily many children over successive
decrease-key operations. Correctness (heap order, the represented multiset, the cached
minimum) does not depend on marks and is fully proved here. The classical amortized
`O(1)` bound for decrease-key and the Fibonacci size bound on trees of a given degree
do depend on marks and cascading cuts; neither is claimed. There is no cost model in
this file, as in the parent module.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.FibonacciHeap.DecreaseKey

module_doc:
# Separate-chaining hash tables

A table has a positive finite bucket count and an explicit hash function. Each bucket is a
canonical `AList` chain, and `HashTable.Valid` requires keys to lie in their hash-selected bucket.

## Main definitions

* `HashTable` stores the bucket count and chains.
* `HashTable.empty`, `HashTable.lookup`, and `HashTable.insert` implement the table operations.
* `HashTable.abstraction` flattens the chains into a bucket-independent Mathlib `Finmap`.

## Main statements

Insertion preserves validity, returns the new value for its key, and preserves other lookups even
when keys collide. For valid tables, lookup and insertion agree with the finite-map abstraction.
No expected-time bound is claimed: the model includes no probability distribution on hashes.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.HashTable

module_doc:
# Indexed binary minimum queue

One canonical binary heap stores lexicographic key/identity pairs. The inverse vector
records each live identity's exact slot; swaps update only the two affected entries.
The five operations preserve the heap and inverse invariants.

The selected event tuple counts comparisons, swaps, inverse reads, inverse writes,
and entry append/pop/replacement. General indexing, allocation, copying, RAM/word/bit
and space refinements are not included. Repeated construction uses source-order INSERT.

Retained Lean is authored/repaired by Codex at Adam Kiezun's explicit selection.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.IndexedMinQueue.Basic

module_doc:
# Selected-event bounds for indexed binary heap operations

Upward recursion reduces parent depth; downward recursion reduces the remaining
child-depth allowance. The bounds concern the exact executed event tuple, not
RAM/word/bit operations or allocation. Repeated construction uses actual INSERT calls.

Retained Lean is authored/repaired by Codex at Adam Kiezun's explicit selection.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.IndexedMinQueue.Complexity

module_doc:
# Indexed minimum queue return specifications

The public laws refine the executed operations to the existing canonical binary heap
and preserve identity membership. All inverse/array proof support remains private.

Retained Lean is authored/repaired by Codex at Adam Kiezun's explicit selection.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.IndexedMinQueue.Correctness

module_doc:
# Balanced interval search trees

This module implements closed intervals in an AVL tree ordered by the low
endpoint and a stable occurrence identifier.  Each nonempty node stores its
subtree height, size, and maximum high endpoint.  A second balanced map locates
an existing identifier before replacement or deletion.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.IntervalTree

module_doc:
# Kd-trees

This file defines a kd-tree over points `Fin d → Int`, following La Rocca,
*Advanced Algorithms and Data Structures*, chapter 9, at the level of the
verified orthogonal range report. Internal nodes store a split axis and a split
value; the points are the leaves. `Valid` records the kd invariant at a node
with axis `a` and split value `s`: every point in the left subtree has
`a`-coordinate at most `s` and every point in the right subtree has
`a`-coordinate at least `s` (points on the split hyperplane may occur on both
sides). Building sorts the points by the current axis, splits the sorted list
in half (a median split), takes the split value from the first point of the
right half, and recurses with the next axis cyclically. The range report for
an axis-aligned box `[lo, hi]` prunes a child when the split value already
separates it from the box, and the main theorem states that the report of a
valid tree is exactly its leaf list filtered by the box predicate.

## Main definitions

* `KdTree.build` builds a tree by alternating-axis median splits.
* `KdTree.Valid` is the split invariant.
* `KdTree.report` lists the points of the tree inside an axis-aligned box.

## Deferred

Nearest-neighbor search, dynamic insertion and rebalancing, and all complexity
bounds are not proved here; no cost model is carried.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.KdTree

module_doc:
# Link-cut trees (functional, specification-level model)

A link-cut tree (Sleator-Tarjan) maintains a forest of rooted trees (the
represented forest) as a disjoint union of preferred paths, each stored in
an auxiliary splay tree keyed by depth in the imperative structure. This
module does not model the auxiliary splay trees. It models only the
represented forest and its preferred-path decomposition, functionally and
at the level of specifications:

* the represented forest is a list of `EulerTourTree.Tree`s;
* the preferred-path decomposition is a list of paths `paths s`, computed
  from the state: the state stores the preferred (solid) edges `s.preferred`,
  each directed from a node to its preferred child (`ParentChild`), and
  `paths s` is the maximal solid chains in each represented tree
  (`treePaths`, built from `decomp`), with vertices incident to no solid edge
  forming singleton paths. This is the usual Sleator-Tarjan preferred-path
  decomposition: `mem_paths_flatMap` and `nodup_paths_flatMap` record that
  it partitions the vertex set of the forest, `pairwise_disjoint_paths` that
  distinct paths are vertex-disjoint, and `isChain_of_mem_paths` that
  consecutive vertices of every path are joined by a represented edge;
* `access x` makes the path from the represented root to `x` (`rootPath`)
  solid: its edges become preferred, the previously preferred edge of each
  vertex on the path is dropped, and every preferred edge whose parent
  endpoint lies off the path is retained (`mem_preferred_access`). Off-path
  preferred paths therefore persist across accesses: in the tree with root
  `1`, children `2 → 4` and `3 → 5`, `access 5` after `access 4` keeps the
  preferred path `[2, 4]` (only the edge `1`-`2` is dropped, replaced by
  `1`-`3`), a regression test in `LinkCutTreeTests`. After `access x`, the
  root-to-`x` path is one of the paths of the decomposition and `x` is its
  last (deepest) vertex, recorded by `access_last`;
* the structural operations preserve represented adjacency: `link x y`
  reroots the tree of `x` at `x` and grafts it as a new child subtree of
  `y` (`rerootAt` then `graftAt`, adding exactly the endpoint edge
  `x`-`y`; a no-op when already connected), `makeRoot x` reroots the tree
  containing `x` at `x` by reversing the edges on the old root-to-`x`
  path (`rerootAt`, every undirected edge kept), `cut x` detaches the
  subtree rooted at `x` and prunes it from the remainder (`pruneAt`,
  every remaining edge kept), and `cutEdge x y` removes the undirected
  edge `x`-`y` by the textbook composite `cut y` after `makeRoot x`,
  guarded by a computable adjacency test (`adjacentB`): on a
  non-adjacent pair it leaves the forest unchanged
  (`cutEdge_eq_of_not_adjacent`). Structural operations reset
  `preferred` to `[]` (all edges dashed).

The abstractions proved here are forest connectivity and the undirected
edge relation: `Connected s x y` is reachability in one represented tree,
equivalently co-occurrence in one Euler tour (`connected_iff_tour`), and
`Adjacent a b t` is parent-child adjacency in a represented tree, with
`adjacent_graftAt` (grafting adds exactly one edge),
`adjacent_rerootAt` (rerooting a duplicate-free tree keeps every edge),
and `adjacent_pruneAt_of_mem_mem` (pruning keeps every edge whose
endpoints survive) specifying the surgeries at the level of edges. The
main theorems are
`connected_link` (a link connects its endpoints), `not_connected_cut` (a cut
separates the detached subtree from the rest of its tree),
`not_connected_cutEdge` and `adjacent_cutEdge` (an edge cut on an
adjacent pair in a valid state separates exactly that pair and retains
every other edge), `access_last`
(`access x` makes `x` the last, deepest vertex of its preferred path),
`makeRoot_root` (`makeRoot x` installs a tree rooted at `x`),
`access_forest`/`connected_access_iff` (`access` changes only preferred
paths), and the invariant-preservation theorems `Valid.access`,
`Valid.makeRoot`, `Valid.link`, `Valid.cut`, and `Valid.cutEdge`.

## What is not modeled

This is not the imperative link-cut tree. Concretely, out of scope here:

* the auxiliary splay trees themselves: no splay-tree shape, root, or
  splaying operation is modeled here. The textbook `expose` operation
  (`access` plus a splay of the auxiliary tree) is therefore not
  modeled either; this module provides `access` (the preferred-path
  update) only. A preferred path is represented solely as its vertex
  list ordered from shallowest to deepest, with no auxiliary-tree
  correctness claim;
* path aggregates and subtree queries;
* a full edge-level specification of `pruneAt`/`cut` as an adjacency
  equivalence: grafting and rerooting are specified at edge level for
  arbitrary vertex pairs (`adjacent_graftAt`, `adjacent_rerootAt`), and
  pruning is specified by edge retention on the surviving vertices
  (`adjacent_pruneAt_of_mem_mem`, with the vertex-set characterizations
  `mem_vertices_pruneAt`, `mem_vertices_pruneAt_of_mem_not_mem`,
  `perm_vertices_pruneAt`); that every edge of the pruned remainder was
  already an edge of the original tree, and a state-level adjacency
  equivalence for the rooted `cut` (as opposed to `cutEdge`, covered by
  `adjacent_cutEdge`), are not proved. The separation/connectivity
  theorems apply as before, together with exact-forest
  composition tests on branched trees in `LinkCutTreeTests` (for example
  linking `1` with children `2`, `3` under an isolated `4` and then
  cutting `2` leaves `{4, 1, 3}` and `{2}` with the original branch
  intact, and `cutEdge 1 2` on the branched tree leaves `{1, 3}` and
  `{2}`);
* all amortized bounds, including the `O(log n)` access lemma.

## Dependency

The represented forest is built from the `EulerTourTree.Tree` API in
`EulerTourTree.lean` (landed separately); this module only consumes
`Tree.vertices`, `Tree.tour`, and the tree structure from it.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.LinkCutTree

module_doc:
# Least-recently-used caches

A list-based LRU cache of capacity `cap`, following the presentation in La Rocca, *Advanced
Algorithms and Data Structures*, Chapter 7. Entries are stored most-recent-first in a list of
key-value pairs. The structure bundles the two invariants: keys are pairwise distinct and the
number of entries never exceeds the capacity.

## Main definitions

* `LruCache` stores the entries together with proofs of the invariants.
* `LruCache.get` looks up a key and promotes its entry to the front on a hit.
* `LruCache.put` inserts or updates a key at the front, dropping entries beyond the capacity.

## Main statements

Lookups hit exactly on stored keys (`get_hit`, `get_miss`), a lookup right after a `put` returns
the stored value (`get_put`), the size and key-uniqueness invariants hold of every cache
(`size_le_cap`, `keys_nodup`), and a key evicted by `put` is the least recently used one
(`evicted_is_least_recent`). State transitions are characterized exactly: `get` permutes the
entries without changing any binding (`get_perm`, `mem_get_entries_iff`, `get_size`), and when
`put` evicts nothing its entries are the new binding plus all surviving old ones
(`mem_put_entries_iff_of_not_full`, `get_put_of_ne`).
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.LruCache

module_doc:
# Open-addressing hash tables

An open-addressing table (CLRS, Section 11.4) stores at most one key-value pair per
slot. The table has `m` slots and a probe sequence `probe k 0, probe k 1, …` per key,
supplied as a parameter. `lookup` walks the key's probe sequence and stops at the
first slot holding the key (success), at the first empty slot (failure), or after `m`
probes (failure). `insert` walks the same sequence and stops at the first slot that
is empty or already holds the key, writing the new binding there; it returns `none`
when the first `m` probes are all occupied by other keys. For probe sequences that
are permutations of the slots, failure is exactly the statement that the table is
full, but no permutation property is assumed here.

## Main definitions

* `OpenAddressing` stores the slots as a `Vector (Option (K × V)) m`.
* `OpenAddressing.empty`, `OpenAddressing.lookup`, and `OpenAddressing.insert`
  implement the table operations by bounded recursion on a fuel of `m` attempts.
* `OpenAddressing.Valid` is the probe-closed invariant plus key uniqueness: every
  stored key is reached by its own probe sequence before any empty slot, and no key
  is stored in two different slots. Uniqueness is what makes `insert` a genuine
  replacement: in a valid table there is no stale second binding for the key.
* `OpenAddressing.linearProbe` and `OpenAddressing.doubleHashProbe` are the usual
  linear-probing and double-hashing probe sequences.

## Specification choice

Unlike separate chaining (`HashTable`), there is no bucket-independent `Finmap`
abstraction: with no uniqueness or permutation assumption on `probe`, the contents
of the table are specified instead by the `Stored` predicate, which states that some
slot holds the given binding; under `Valid` the binding for a key is unique
(`stored_unique`). The main correctness statements are that a successful
insert is found by `lookup` with the inserted value, that insertion preserves
`Valid`, that under `Valid` a lookup returns `some value` if and only if
`Stored table key value` (`lookup_eq_some_iff`), and that an insert leaves
every other key's stored binding and lookup unchanged (`stored_insert_of_ne`,
`lookup_insert_of_ne`).

Deletion is out of scope. Clearing a slot breaks probe-closedness for keys stored
later along the same probe sequence; CLRS repairs searches with a `DELETED`
tombstone marker, which this model does not have.

No expected-time bound is claimed: the model supplies neither a probability
distribution nor a uniform-hashing assumption about `probe`.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.OpenAddressing

module_doc:
# Order-statistic binary search trees

This module augments Mathlib's `BinaryTree` carrier with a cached subtree size at
each node. Its ordering, traversal, membership, rank, and select specifications
are inherited from `BinarySearchTree` through `erase`.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.OrderStatisticTree

module_doc:
# Order-statistic tree deletion

Key deletion for the size-augmented tree of `OrderStatisticTree.lean`. The name
`erase` already denotes cache-stripping there, so deletion is called `delete`.

Deletion follows the search path, rebuilding ancestors with the cache-repairing
constructor `node`; at the deleted node the two subtrees are combined with
`merge`. Order, membership, traversal, rank, and select specifications are
inherited from `BinarySearchTree` through `erase`, following the parent module.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.OrderStatisticTree.Delete

module_doc:
# Ordered insertion into a list

`orderedInsert x xs` inserts `x` into `xs` at its sorted position. On a
strictly sorted list (`xs.Pairwise (· < ·)`) this returns `xs` unchanged
when `x` is already present (`orderedInsert_eq_of_mem`); on an arbitrary
list the scan stops at the first element not smaller than `x`, so a
duplicate occurring later is not detected — for example
`orderedInsert 2 [3, 2] = [2, 3, 2]`. The tree implementations in this
library (2-3 trees and B-trees) only apply it to strictly sorted
flattenings, whose flattening lemmas state that tree insertion acts on
the inorder flattening by `orderedInsert`.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.OrderedInsert

module_doc:
# Perfect hashing (two-level static scheme)

A static set of keys can be stored with worst-case constant lookup time by the
two-level scheme of Fredman, Komlós, and Szemerédi, presented in CLRS,
Section 11.5. A primary hash function sends each key to one of several buckets. Each
bucket `i` holding `nᵢ` keys gets its own secondary table of size `mᵢ = nᵢ²` and its
own secondary hash function that is *injective* on the keys of that bucket, so a lookup
probes exactly one secondary slot and never follows a chain or a probe sequence.

This file models the scheme as data with a correctness predicate. `PerfectHashing`
stores the bucket count, the secondary table sizes and hash functions, and the
secondary tables themselves. `PerfectHashing.Valid` requires every stored binding to
sit in the slot selected by the two hash functions for its key, plus injectivity of
each secondary hash on the keys stored in its bucket. The injectivity clause is
implied by the placement clause (two stored keys at the same secondary slot would
have to share a single slot), which is `Valid.injective_of_placed`; it is kept as a
separate field because it is the property the FKS construction has to achieve when
choosing the secondary hash functions.

## Main statements

* `lookup_eq_some_of_stored` and `stored_of_lookup_eq_some`: under `Valid`, lookup
  succeeds with value `v` for key `k` exactly when some slot stores `(k, v)`. The
  slot contents are equivalently described by the list abstraction `entries`
  (`mem_entries_iff`), with corollaries `lookup_eq_some_of_mem_entries` and
  `mem_entries_of_lookup_eq_some`. Stored values are unique (`stored_unique`), so
  the contents form a partial function from keys to values.
* `totalSecondarySpace` is `∑ i, mᵢ`, the total number of secondary slots. Under the
  FKS sizing rule `SquareSized` (`mᵢ = nᵢ²` for every bucket), it equals
  `∑ i, nᵢ²` (`totalSecondarySpace_eq_sum_sq`) and is at most the square of the total
  number of keys (`totalSecondarySpace_le_totalKeys_sq`).

## What is not proved here

The existence theorems of the FKS method are out of scope. CLRS shows that a primary
hash function with `∑ i, nᵢ² = O(n)` exists and can be found by random sampling from
a universal family, and that for each bucket a collision-free secondary hash into
`nᵢ²` slots exists because a random universal hash is injective on `nᵢ` keys with
probability at least `1 / 2`. Those arguments are probabilistic counting over a hash
family (Markov's inequality applied to expected collision counts). Collision counting
for a universal family (such as the mod-prime family) is a prerequisite for that work
but is not developed or used here; neither that counting nor the linear-space bound
is claimed in this module.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.PerfectHashing

module_doc:
# Amortized cost of `Std.Queue`

This file equips Lean's two-list queue with a `TimeM Nat` cost model. Enqueueing costs one unit.
Dequeueing costs one unit plus the length of the enqueue list exactly when that list is reversed.
The potential is the enqueue-list length, making the amortized charges two for enqueue and one for
dequeue.

The costs describe this explicit model, not compiler or wall-clock time.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.Queue.Amortized

module_doc:
# FIFO semantics for `Std.Queue`

This file exposes the logical FIFO sequence represented by Lean's two-list queue and proves the
behavior of the basic queue operations against that sequence. It makes no complexity claims.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.Queue.Semantics

module_doc:
# Radix tries (Patricia tries)

A radix trie compresses a trie by labelling edges with nonempty lists instead of single
symbols (La Rocca, *Advanced Algorithms and Data Structures*, ch. 6). A node stores an
optional value, so a key may end at an internal node, together with a list of
`(label, subtree)` children. In a valid trie every label is nonempty, first symbols of
sibling labels are distinct, every subtree is valid, and every non-root node is
path-compressed: a node storing no value has at least two children, so no unary
value-free node could be merged into its parent edge. Lookup follows the child whose
label starts with the next key symbol and requires the whole label to be a prefix of the
remaining key. Insertion walks to the edge sharing the key's first symbol and splits that
edge at the longest common prefix of key and label: if both continue past the common
prefix, a new internal node with no value branches to the old subtree and a new leaf.
Children use a raw association list because Lean cannot nest recursively valued tries in
`AList`; `Valid` records the invariant. The abstraction is `entries`, the flattened
key-value list in stored sibling order, and lookup is characterized against it for valid
tries. No complexity bounds are proved.

## Prefix search, bulk construction, and key uniqueness

Generic `RadixTrie` API (moved here from the suffix-tree module, which is a
client of it): prefix search (`hasPrefix`) and its correctness against
`keys`, building a trie from a list of pairs (`buildFrom`) with lookup and
key characterizations, and duplicate-freeness of stored keys
(`Valid.keys_nodup`).
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.RadixTrie

module_doc:
# Range trees (1D)

This file defines a one-dimensional range tree over `Int`, following Demaine's
MIT 6.851 lecture 3 at the level of the verified report operation. The tree is a
balanced binary tree built from a list by recursively splitting it in half.
Each node caches the interval `[lo, hi]` spanned by its leaves, so the
pruning test at a node is constant-time (`tmin`/`tmax` are projections, not
recomputed traversals); `BoundsOk` records that the cached interval is the
true leaf interval, and the report theorem is stated for `BoundsOk` trees.
The classical leaf-order convention is the separate ordering invariant in
`Valid` (bounds plus sorted leaf list); `build` preserves the input order
verbatim, so `valid_build_of_sorted` gives `Valid (build xs)` under an
explicit `xs.Pairwise (· ≤ ·)` hypothesis — `build [2, 1]` is bounds-valid but
not `Valid`, and no theorem here identifies it with a sorted range tree.
A range report for `[lo, hi]`
prunes a node whose interval is disjoint from `[lo, hi]`, takes a node whose
interval is contained in `[lo, hi]` whole (the canonical-node step), and
otherwise recurses into both children. The main theorem states that the report
is exactly the inorder leaf list filtered to `[lo, hi]`; counting is the length
of the report.

## Main definitions

* `RangeTree.build` builds a balanced tree from a list by halving.
* `RangeTree.report` lists the stored values in `[lo, hi]`.
* `RangeTree.count` counts the stored values in `[lo, hi]`.

## Deferred

The two-dimensional layered range tree with fractional cascading, dynamic
updates, and all complexity bounds (`O(log n)` canonical nodes, and so on) are
not proved here; no cost model is carried.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.RangeTree

module_doc:
# Red-black trees

This module develops pure functional red-black trees with Okasaki's insertion.
The invariants are the usual ones, stated separately: `Ordered` is the strict
binary-search-tree invariant, inherited from `BinarySearchTree` through the
color-erasing projection `erase` (as in `OrderStatisticTree`), `RedOk` forbids a
red node with a red child, and `Balanced` states that every root-to-leaf path
contains the same number of black nodes, where the count along the left spine
is computed by `blackHeight`. A tree is `Valid` when it satisfies all three
invariants and has a black root. Membership, `All`, and inorder traversal are
likewise inherited through `erase`; only the color invariants, `blackHeight`,
and Okasaki's rebalancing insertion are red-black-specific.

Insertion follows Okasaki: an unchecked insertion `ins` may create a red-red
redex at the root (the relaxed invariant `AlmostRedOk`), `balance` repairs a
redex below a black node, and the public `insert` recolors the root black.
Insertion preserves `blackHeight` exactly before the final recoloring, which
can raise it by one.

Deletion is out of scope for this module and is a staged follow-up.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.RedBlackTree

module_doc:
# Red-black tree deletion

Deletion for the red-black trees of
`CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.RedBlackTree`, in two stages.
First, `del` is the ordinary unbalanced binary-search-tree deletion: it
follows comparisons from the root and splices the two subtrees of a deleted
node together with `join`, ignoring colors, so the result need not satisfy
`RedOk` or `Balanced`. Second, `rebalance` rebuilds a valid red-black tree
from the inorder traversal of the intermediate tree by repeated Okasaki
insertion (`fromList`), whose validity is already established in the parent
module. The public `delete` is the composite: it satisfies the same inorder
specification as unbalanced deletion (`inorder_delete`), removes exactly the
deleted key (`mem_delete`), and always produces a `Valid` tree
(`valid_delete`). The traversal and membership specifications assume the
strict invariant `Ordered`, matching `contains_eq_true_iff` in the parent
module.

This delete-by-rebuild takes linearithmic time in the size of the tree, not
the logarithmic time of a double-black (Kahrs) deletion that repairs the
black-height invariant locally along the search path; the staged invariant
proofs here deliberately reuse `valid_fromList` instead of a local repair.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.RedBlackTree.Delete

module_doc:
# Red-black tree deletion by double-black bubbles

Logarithmic deletion for the red-black trees of
`CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.RedBlackTree`, by the classic
double-black (Kahrs) method. Unlike `RedBlackTree.delete`, which
rebuilds the whole tree from its inorder traversal, `deleteBal` here repairs
the black-height invariant locally along the search path.

A deletion that removes a black node leaves its subtree one black node short
on every root-to-leaf path. The shortfall is represented by a *double-black*
root: the auxiliary type `BBTree` is either a genuine tree (`.regular`), a
double-black empty tree (`.emptyBB`, the result of deleting a black leaf), or
a double-black node (`.nodeBB`) whose children are genuine trees. Only the
root of a `BBTree` can be double black; this bubble invariant is built into
the type, since the children of `.nodeBB` have the parent module's type
`Tree`. The extended root color is `BColor`, with `.doubleBlack` counting as
two black nodes for `bhBB`, so a balanced tree and its double-black
counterpart have the same `bhBB` as the original `blackHeight`.

The core `del` descends once from the root. When the recursive result is
double black, `balLeft`/`balRight` (through `fixLeft`/`fixRight`) repair it
against its sibling: a red far nephew is repaired by a single rotation, a red
near nephew by a double rotation, and two black nephews by reddening the
sibling and bubbling the double black to the parent (a red sibling is first
rotated to the parent's place, reducing to the black-sibling cases under a
red parent). Deleting a node with two children promotes its successor, the
minimum key of the right subtree. The public `deleteBal` finishes with
`blacken`, which absorbs a remaining double black at the root. Every step
except the single descent touches O(1) nodes, so `deleteBal` visits
O(height) nodes.

The specifications match `RedBlackTree.Delete`, with their preconditions
kept distinct: for an ordered tree (`Ordered tree`),
`inorder_deleteBal` erases the key from the inorder traversal and
`mem_deleteBal` removes exactly the deleted key; for a tree satisfying
the three structural invariants `Ordered`, `RedOk`, and `Balanced`,
`valid_deleteBal_of_invariants` concludes that the result again
satisfies the red-black invariants (the input root need not be black),
and `valid_deleteBal` wraps it for `Valid tree`. Deleting from a tree
without the structural invariants need not produce a valid one.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.RedBlackTree.DeleteBalanced

module_doc:
# Segment trees

This file defines a segment tree over a list with values in an additive monoid;
the aggregate of a list is its `List.sum`, accumulated from left to right, so no
commutativity is required. Each internal node caches the aggregate and the length
of its segment, and `Valid` records that every cached aggregate equals the sum of
the children's aggregates and every cached length equals the sum of the children's
lengths, so split positions are available in constant time. The index set of a tree
is the inorder leaf list `toList`. A range query over `[l, r)` returns the sum of
the slice `(toList.drop l).take (r - l)`; it prunes empty, left-disjoint, and
right-disjoint segments, uses cached aggregates for fully covered nodes, and clamps
out-of-range bounds through the slice. Point update replaces the in-range leaf at
an index and leaves the leaf list unchanged out of range. Building splits the list
in half recursively, evaluating each recursive build once. No complexity bounds
are proved.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.SegmentTree

module_doc:
# Singly-linked lists over a node pool

A `Node` has a payload and an optional next pointer; `none` denotes NIL.
As in `DoublyLinkedList.Basic`, an allocated node pool is a
`Vector (Option (Node α (Fin capacity))) capacity`, and `Represents` relates a
pool and a header to an ordered list of distinct node identities, here with
next pointers only.

The operations are plain functions on the pool (no cost model): `prepend`
links an already allocated node at the head, `insertAfter` links an allocated
node after a given node, `deleteHead` drops the head, and `deleteAfter`
splices out the successor of a given node. Each operation comes with a
pointwise store equation and a `Represents` correctness theorem describing how
the represented identity list changes. `contents` collects the payloads stored
at a list of identities, and `search` follows next pointers with an explicit
fuel bound (the public wrapper uses the pool capacity), returning the first
identity whose payload equals the target.

Freshness of a linked-in node is a premise of the representation proofs, not
an execution guard, matching the doubly-linked list development.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList

module_doc:
# Deterministic skip lists

This module models a finite skip list by a sorted bottom list whose nodes carry positive tower
heights. `level i` selects the nodes whose towers reach level `i`; consequently every upper level
is a subsequence of the level below it. Search descends from the greatest level while carrying the
suffix after the last visible predecessor, so every lower scan starts from the narrowed window.

Insertion takes an explicit height, separating deterministic correctness from any random promotion
policy. A zero requested height is normalized to one. Reinserting a key replaces its value while
preserving its old tower height. This list reference implementation takes `O(n * (H + 1))`
comparisons in the worst case for `n` nodes and maximum height `H`; upper-level progress can narrow
later scans, but no expected logarithmic bound is claimed.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.SkipList

module_doc:
# Sparse tables

A sparse table answers range-minimum queries over a static list. The operation must be
idempotent so that two overlapping intervals can jointly cover a query interval: the overlap
is counted twice, and idempotence absorbs the double count. We use `min` over a linear
order, the simplest idempotent operation; idempotence is `min_self`.

Level `k` of the table stores, at each start index `i` with `i + 2 ^ k ≤ n`, the minimum of
the length-`2 ^ k` slice starting at `i`; level `k + 1` combines adjacent level-`k` entries
against the level dropped by `2 ^ k`. The list function `level` states this specification,
while the built table stores its levels in an `Array (Array α)` so that `entry` is random
access, and `build` computes each level once from the single retained previous row. The
built table has `Nat.log2 n + 1` levels. A query over `[l, r)` with `k = Nat.log2 (r - l)`
returns the minimum of the two length-`2 ^ k` slices starting at `l` and at `r - 2 ^ k`,
which overlap and cover `[l, r)`. Slice minima in the public specification are the
canonical `List.min?` (`none` for the empty slice), so an empty query interval returns
`none`; internally the proofs use a private right-fold minimum that is proved equal to
`List.min?` and is not exported. Queries are proved correct whenever `r ≤ n`,
including reversed bounds `r ≤ l`, where both the query and the slice minimum
are `none`.
No complexity bounds are proved; the model carries no cost instrumentation.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.SparseTable

module_doc:
# Splay trees

Self-adjusting binary search trees (Sleator-Tarjan), following Demaine's
MIT 6.851 Lecture 5. The carrier is Mathlib's `BinaryTree`, reusing
`BinarySearchTree.inorder`, `BinarySearchTree.All`,
`BinarySearchTree.Ordered` and structural membership from
`BinarySearchTree`.

`splay x t` is the bottom-up splay: search for `x` as in a binary search
tree, then rotate the found node (or the last node visited) to the root
with the three double-rotation cases: zig (single rotation at the root),
zig-zig (rotate the grandparent-parent edge first), and zig-zag (rotate
the parent-node edge first). The definition pattern-matches two levels
of the tree at once, recursing into the relevant grandchild. `insert`
splays the key and then splits, `access` splays and reports whether the
key reached the root, and `contains` is its Boolean projection.

The module proves functional correctness only: splaying preserves the
inorder traversal (hence membership and `Ordered`), and a present key
ends at the root. The amortized `O(log n)` access lemma (the
Sleator-Tarjan potential argument) is out of scope.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.SplayTree

module_doc:
# Standalone stack operations

The existing top-first `List` carrier is unchanged. A successful PUSH, POP,
or TOP counts one selected stack event; underflow returns `none` and costs
zero. Guards, allocation, copying and machine instructions are not charged.
The existing MULTIPOP and sequence cost convention is unchanged.

This first additive increment was authored by Codex at Adam Kiezun's
selection.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.Stack.Basic

module_doc:
# MULTIPOP and its aggregate cost

CLRS, fourth edition, Section 16.1 (printed pages 449–450). A list stores the
stack with its top first. The loop removes one element while the stack is
nonempty and the requested count is positive. Integer requests at most zero
leave the stack unchanged.

CSLib's `TimeM` counts one event for each actual POP and one for each PUSH.
Guards, decrements, allocation and copying are not charged. This is the
source's abstract stack-operation cost, not a RAM or native runtime bound.
Successful operation sequences have cost at most twice their length plus
the initial stack size; empty POP returns an error and stops the sequence.

Retained Lean was authored by Codex at Adam Kiezun's explicit selection.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.Stack.Multipop

module_doc:
# Suffix arrays

This file defines the suffix array of a list over a linearly ordered alphabet: the
starting indices of the suffixes, sorted by the suffixes themselves in lexicographic
order. The array is a permutation of `List.range s.length`, and mapping each index to
its suffix gives a pairwise sorted list. The longest-common-prefix length `lcp` is
defined directly on lists over any alphabet with decidable equality (no order is
needed), with its basic bounds, symmetry, agreement on the common-prefix
truncation, and a maximality characterization
(`le_lcp_iff : q ≤ lcp x y ↔ q ≤ min x.length y.length ∧ x.take q = y.take q`)
showing it is the *longest* such length, not merely an agreeing one. Only
suffix sorting and `lcpArray` require the linear order. The `lcpArray`
records the LCP length of each pair of adjacent suffixes in suffix-array order.

Suffixes here are the non-empty suffixes `s.drop i` for `i < s.length`; `suffixes`
is `List.tails`, which additionally ends with the empty suffix.

Out of scope: the linear-time Kasai construction of the LCP array and any linear or
near-linear suffix-array construction (the definition uses `List.mergeSort` with
suffix comparison, so no complexity bound is claimed). Suffix trees are out of scope
for this module; a suffix-tree representation belongs in its own module with a
source-indexed validity predicate and construction.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.SuffixArray

module_doc:
# Suffix trees

The suffix tree of a list `s` is the radix (Patricia) trie of all suffixes of the
terminated string `s.map some ++ [none]`, over the alphabet `Option α` with `none` as a
fresh terminator (each terminated suffix contains `none` only at its end, so as strings
no terminated suffix is a prefix of another). Each suffix is stored with its starting
index as the value, so the stored keys are exactly the `s.length + 1` suffixes of the
terminated string, and exact lookup of a suffix returns its starting index. The API
is stated about stored keys; identifying them with the structural leaves of the trie
(the value-bearing nodes with no children) is not formalized here.

Pattern search is prefix lookup: `RadixTrie.hasPrefix` walks the trie following the edge
sharing the pattern's first symbol, succeeding when the pattern ends inside an edge or
at a node above stored keys. The main theorems state that `(suffixTree s).hasPrefix
(p.map some)` holds exactly when `p` is a prefix of some suffix of `s`, and equivalently
when `p <:+: s`.

The generic `RadixTrie` facts the construction needs — prefix search and its
correctness against `keys`, building a trie from a list of pairs (`buildFrom`)
with lookup and key characterizations, and duplicate-freeness of stored keys —
live in `RadixTrie.lean` with the rest of the radix-trie API, so radix-trie
clients do not import suffix-tree or suffix-array code.

Construction is naive insertion of all suffixes, taking quadratic total input length in
`s.length`. Out of scope: the linear-time Ukkonen construction, suffix links, a
structural characterization of trie leaves (and their coincidence with the stored
keys), and any in-order correspondence with the suffix array. The construction here
is the suffix-tree representation; it reuses `RadixTrie` directly, and no separate
compact-trie node type is exported.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.SuffixTree

module_doc:
# Treaps

This module defines deterministic treap operations. Each node stores an explicit
priority; no correctness theorem depends on a random source. Insertion and
deletion are implemented from key splitting and priority-guided merging.

The implementation and proofs were authored for this module. The representation
style follows `BinarySearchTree` from D123980084; no public treap implementation
was copied.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.Treap

module_doc:
# Finite tries

This file defines a finite trie whose keys are lists over a decidable alphabet. A node stores an
optional value independently of its children, so a key may end at an internal prefix. Child keys
are unique in a valid trie; lookup-equivalence is the semantic abstraction when sibling order
differs. The order of `entries` follows the stored sibling order. Children use a raw association
list because Lean cannot nest recursively valued tries in `AList`; `Valid` records key uniqueness.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.Trie

module_doc:
# Trie deletion

Deletion for the finite tries of `CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.Trie`.
`delete` unmarks the terminal node of the deleted key and prunes childless
non-terminal nodes on the way back up: when the recursively updated child
carries no value and no children, its entry is dropped from the parent
altogether. The pruning step replaces the first entry at the updated key
in place and drops any later duplicates at that key, so the order of the
surviving entries (and hence of `entries`) is preserved and the lookup
specifications hold for arbitrary tries, with no `Valid` hypothesis;
`Valid.delete` separately records that deletion preserves the invariant.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.Trie.Delete

module_doc:
# 2-3 trees

A 2-3 tree is a balanced search tree in which every internal node has two or
three children and all leaves lie at the same depth. Here the tree type is
indexed by its height: a `Tree α h` has all of its leaves at depth `h`, so
balance is a typing invariant. The recursive `Balanced` predicate and
`height_eq` record the same fact at the level of the recursively computed
height. Keys stored at nodes are strict separators: in `node2 a l r` every key
of `l` is below `a` and every key of `r` is above it, and similarly with two
separators at a `node3`; this is the `Ordered` predicate.

Insertion follows the standard splitting discipline. The auxiliary `ins`
returns an `Overflow`: either a replacement tree of the same height, or a
*split* into two trees of that height separated by a promoted key. A 2-node
absorbs a split child by becoming a 3-node; a 3-node passes a split upward.
At the root, a split becomes a new 2-node and the height grows by one.
Insertion ignores an already-present key.

The machine-checked results are `ins_spec`, which bundles preservation of
`Ordered` and the equation `flatten (insert result) = orderedInsert x (flatten
t)` for the height-indexed insertion, and its root-level consequences in the
`Root` API: `Root.ordered_insert`, `Root.flatten_insert`,
`Root.mem_flatten_insert`, and `Root.contains_eq_true_iff` (search agrees with
membership in the flattening). There is no formal cost model; the index gives
height `O(log n)` only in combination with size bounds that are not stated
here. Deletion is out of scope for this module.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.TwoThreeTree

module_doc:
# Persistent union-find with parent-path costs

This module models a finite parent forest. A `Forest n` stores one parent and a
natural-number depth certificate for every `Fin n`; every non-root parent edge
strictly decreases that certificate. `find` follows parent pointers to a root.

`union` is persistent: it links the root of the first class to the root of the
second class. It deliberately models neither union-by-rank nor path compression.
The explicit `TimeM Nat` model charges one unit per vertex visited by `find` and
one additional unit for a root link only when the two representatives are
distinct (no link is performed, or charged, when they already coincide). Thus
`find` is bounded by certified forest depth, and `union` by the two searches
plus at most one. These are abstract operation counts, not compiler or
wall-clock costs.
name: CSLibExt.Algorithms.Lean.DataStructures.UnionFind

module_doc:
# Connected components using the canonical union-find

CLRS fourth edition, section 19.1, printed pages 522–523. This executes
CONNECTED-COMPONENTS with canonical Batteries UnionFind, union by rank and
path compression. Edges retain their input order, loops and duplicates.

The direct CSLib TimeM annotation counts MAKE-SET, FIND-SET and UNION calls:
(n, 2 * edges.length, n - number of graph components). A checked query performs
two FIND-SET calls and its carried store is retained even when UNION is skipped.
These are source call counts, not parent-visit, alpha, RAM, bit or space bounds.
